history: Congress designated the Rio Chama a Wild and Scenic River in 1988. The first 24.6 miles from El Vado are designated; the lower section is a study river.
The river runs through a multi-colored sandstone canyon up to 1,500 feet deep, with heavily wooded side canyons, historic sites and dinosaur tracks.

Spanish colonial authorities founded Abiquiú in 1754 as a settlement for genízaros, Native people who had been taken from their communities and raised in Spanish households. In 1829 it became the starting point of the Old Spanish Trail to California.
The Benedictine Monastery of Christ in the Desert, founded in 1964, sits on the river just above Chavez Canyon at the end of a long dirt road. It marks the end of the wild upper river.

The painter Georgia O’Keeffe made the cliffs and badlands around Ghost Ranch and Abiquiú famous in the 1930s and after. The red, yellow and white cliffs she painted are cut from similar layers to the walls you float past.

El Vado Dam, built in 1935, stores water for irrigation downstream on the Rio Grande and now also holds San Juan–Chama project water. Abiquiu Dam, completed in 1963, backs up the lower river into Abiquiu Lake, which begins near the Big Eddy take-out.
The Chama River Canyon Wilderness was created by Congress on February 24, 1978, ten years before the river was added to the Wild and Scenic system.
indigenous: The Chama valley is part of the traditional homeland of the Tewa-speaking Pueblo peoples, whose ancestors built villages along the river and its tributaries. Poshuouinge, a large ancestral Tewa pueblo ruin, lies near Abiquiú. Ute, Navajo and Jicarilla Apache groups also used the area. Treat every sherd, wall and rock-art panel as part of a living cultural landscape.
geology: The walls show the Mesozoic section of the Colorado Plateau: red Chinle mudstones from the Triassic, about 215 million years old, at the base; pale Jurassic Entrada sandstone above; and, farther down toward Abiquiú, white Todilto limestone and gypsum capping the Entrada. The dinosaur tracks reached from Jurassic Park camp are preserved in this Mesozoic stack. Sandstone cliffs up to 1,500 feet high enclose the river.
flows: The early season runs April 15 to July 15 and the release season runs July 16 to September 15, when the float depends on scheduled releases from the dam. In winter the flow can be about 50 cfs, which is not boatable.

rules.d: A Coast Guard approved Type I, III or V life jacket for every person, plus one spare per group.
A bailing device on each non-self-bailing craft, and a throw line of at least 50 ft on each boat over 10 ft. A rope at least as long as the boat.
A first-aid kit, patching and repair equipment, and an air pump for inflatables.
All fires must be in a fire pan with 2-inch sides and at least 12 inches across. Carry out all ashes and coals. Lightweight stoves have much less impact.

Solid human waste must be carried out in a washable, reusable container. Plastic bags are not allowed, except bag systems for very small groups. Strain liquid kitchen waste into the river. Empty your toilet at an RV dump station (Espanola, Santa Fe, Taos or Durango).
Dogs must be leashed and under control at all times, and their waste carried out.
Choose an established site, stay on durable surfaces, and keep pollutants out of the water. Collect only dead and down wood.
There are no facilities on the river. Restrooms and drinking water are at El Vado Ranch only.
Forest Road 151 to Chavez Canyon and Big Eddy is dirt and can be impassable when wet.
About 50 miles each way. Up the Creek Shuttle Service: 505-490-2052.
Flows come from El Vado Dam and change with water-delivery and irrigation schedules, so check the Rio Chama below El Vado Dam gauge before you launch and again during the trip.
Water released from the dam runs cold even in summer. Dress for immersion.

landmarks.name: El Vado Ranch put-in
landmarks.desc: River left. The main launch for multiday floats through the Chama Canyon Wilderness, just below El Vado Dam. Fee parking, cabins and a small store. Private launch fee.

landmarks.name: Christ in the Desert Monastery
landmarks.desc: The monastery stands above the river just above Chavez Canyon. The wild upper river ends here.

landmarks.name: Chavez Canyon boat launch
landmarks.desc: River left, off Forest Road 151, with limited parking and a vault toilet. Take-out of the wilderness run, and the put-in for a no-permit day run to Big Eddy.

landmarks.name: Chama Campground
landmarks.desc: An alternate access for small craft. No ramp.

landmarks.name: Skull Bridge
landmarks.desc: A Continental Divide Trail crossing and a possible access.

landmarks.name: USGS gauge 08286500
landmarks.desc: The primary flow reference, Rio Chama above Abiquiu Reservoir.

landmarks.name: Big Eddy take-out
landmarks.desc: River left, off Forest Road 151. Open year-round. A long diagonal shoal about half a mile above can cause hang-ups at low flow.

notes.camp: *Choose an established site on durable ground. There are no facilities on the river, and every group carries out its solid human waste. Side canyons can flash flood.
notes.hike: *Dark Canyon and the other side-canyon hikes are dry washes that flash flood. Dinosaur tracks are protected: look, photograph and leave them as they are.

permit.status: Required April 15 to Sept 15 · lottery for weekends

items.d: An advance permit is required from April 15 to September 15 for launches at El Vado Ranch (the Wild portion, through Chavez Canyon). A day run from Chavez Canyon to Big Eddy needs no permit or fee, only a boater registration form at the launch.

Friday and Saturday launches are assigned by lottery on Recreation.gov. Applications run December 1 to January 31. The lottery awards Friday launches, and winners may launch on Friday or Saturday. You can apply for each season separately.
Sunday through Thursday launches, and unclaimed weekend dates, open on Recreation.gov on April 1 at 8 a.m.
Early season runs April 15 to July 15. Release season runs July 16 to September 15.
You can print it 14 days before launch, and cannot change it afterward. Bring the permit and photo ID to the launch inspection.
Before April 15 and after September 15 no reservation is needed: fill out a self-permit envelope and pay at the put-in. Winter flows can be about 50 cfs, which is not boatable.
Reported by an aggregator: Fridays 6 (early) or 7 (release), Saturdays 6 or 4, Sunday and Monday 2 or 3, Tuesday and Wednesday 1 or 3, Thursday 1. Confirm on Recreation.gov.
Up to 16 people between El Vado Ranch and Chavez Canyon, with at most 2 dogs counted in the group. There is no group limit from Chavez Canyon to Big Eddy.
The permit holder must be at least 18 and present at the launch. One permit per person per season, and permits are not transferable. Private, non-commercial use only.

A $6 non-refundable lottery application fee and $5 per person per launch are reported. At least one person's fee must be paid to accept a lottery award. Cooper's El Vado Ranch charges its own per-person launch fee and a parking fee.

Cancel 14 or more days before launch for a refund of the recreation fee (less the $6). There is no refund inside 13 days. Cancel at least 5 days before launch to avoid a no-show penalty. Dates cannot be changed; cancel and rebook.
Permit violations may bring a 3-year suspension.
About 300 cfs for kayaks, canoes and rafts under 12 ft. Small rafts 300 to 400. Rafts over 12 ft need about 500 cfs. A canoe or kayak can get through to Chavez Canyon at 200 cfs.
Flows come from El Vado Dam and are not guaranteed. Release-season weekends are augmented to about 500 cfs; weekdays can be as low as 80 to 100 cfs.

stats.season: Permits cover April 15 to September 15. Releases from the dam carry the late season, July 16 to September 15.

flow.note: BLM recommends at least 300 cfs for kayaks, canoes and rafts under 12 feet, and 500 for larger rafts. Winter flows can be about 50 cfs, which is not boatable.
